passage:
The power went out just as Aparna and her father, Akash, started the argument again, so they sat in the dark with one candle between them.
"Last Sunday you said I could go to the late show if I finished my project," Aparna said. "Your exact words."
"I said we'd discuss it once the project was done," Akash said. "I would never promise a late show."
Both were certain. Aparna remembered his smile, because she had been so happy that day. Akash remembered feeling uneasy, because he had worried all week about the last bus home.
In the candlelight, Aparna's younger brother spoke up. "I was there. Nobody said 'late show'. You both said 'maybe'."
They looked at each other. Neither spoke for a moment. Then Akash said, "Let's decide it now, and write it down."

qa.q: What did Aparna say her father had promised last Sunday?
qa.a: She said he had promised she could go to the late show if she finished her project.

qa.q: Why does Aparna remember a clear promise?
qa.a: She was so happy that day that she remembered his smile, and her hopes seem to have turned a "maybe" into a yes in her memory.

qa.q: What choice at the end could prevent the next argument like this?
qa.a: Akash suggests deciding now and writing it down, so the plan no longer depends on two memories coloured by feelings.

qa.q: How might the younger brother feel stepping into the argument?
qa.a: He might feel nervous about contradicting both of them, but also that someone had to say what he heard, since each was so sure.

grounding: It shows a teenager and a parent who each remember an argument differently, shaped by hope on one side and worry on the other.

passage:
"You called me useless," Vishal said, dropping his bag by the shoe rack. "On Tuesday. About the maths marks."
Usha, his mother, put down the vegetable knife. "I said the marks were useless for the effort you'd put in. I didn't call you anything."
The argument had happened in the kitchen of their flat in a crowded Chennai colony, with the pressure cooker whistling. Vishal had lain awake that night going over it, and each time the word sounded harsher. Usha had spent the week thinking about how gently she had tried to speak, and her memory had grown gentler too.
Neither of them was lying, and neither could prove a thing.
"Maybe the cooker was loud," Usha said at last. "What I meant was that I know you can do better. I'm sorry it came out like that."
Vishal nodded slowly.

qa.q: Where did the argument about the maths marks happen?
qa.a: It happened in the kitchen of their flat, with the pressure cooker whistling.

qa.q: Why does Vishal remember being called useless?
qa.a: He went over the argument again and again that night, and each time the word sounded harsher, so hurt feelings reshaped the memory.

qa.q: What choice by Usha eased things?
qa.a: Instead of proving her version, Usha allowed that the cooker was loud, explained what she meant and said sorry for how it came out.

qa.q: How has Usha's week of thinking shaped her own memory of Tuesday?
qa.a: She kept thinking about how gently she had tried to speak, so her memory grew gentler too, which made Vishal's version sound unfair to her.

grounding: It shows a teenage son and his mother remembering the same argument differently, each version shaped by later feelings and thoughts.

passage: I'm Pankaj, and this is about the fight over the cricket camp in Ooty. Last month I asked my mother, Uma, if I could go. I remember it exactly: she was at the stove, she didn't even turn round, and she said, "Forget it. You're never going to these camps." I slammed my door so hard the calendar fell. Two weeks later I brought it up again, still angry. Mummy looked shocked. "I said not this year, because of your boards. I said next summer, definitely." She remembered wiping her hands and turning to look at me. We were both completely sure. Then my sister Juhi said from the sofa, "I was there. She said 'not this year'. And you were already walking away." I still feel that "never" in my chest. But maybe my anger wrote that word in afterwards.

qa.q: What was the fight about?
qa.a: The cricket camp in Ooty.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj still feel the "never" even after hearing Juhi?
qa.a: The hurt and anger of that moment shaped the memory, so the harsher word still feels real even if it wasn't said 😔

qa.q: What turning point does Pankaj reach, and what could help in the next argument?
qa.a: Pankaj admits anger may have added the word; next time Pankaj could calmly check, "Did you mean never, or not now?", before walking away.

qa.q: How might Uma feel hearing that Pankaj remembered "never"?
qa.a: She was shocked and probably hurt, since she thought she had promised next summer and turned to look her child in the eye.

passage:
Counsellor's note, family session, Thursday
Parveen and her son Imran (16) came in about an argument from last Friday. Imran is certain she said, "If you fail maths again, don't bother coming home." Parveen is equally certain she said, "If you fail maths again, we need to talk about the phone." Both became tearful describing it. Imran remembers her shouting; Parveen remembers speaking quietly because the neighbours were over. Neither seems to be lying. Each memory looks shaped by what they felt then and what they feared afterwards.
What I did next: I asked each to begin with "I remember it this way", while the other just listened. Then I asked Parveen what she wants Imran to know now. She said, "You can always come home." Imran looked at the floor and nodded.

qa.q: What does Imran remember his mother saying?
qa.a: "If you fail maths again, don't bother coming home."

qa.q: Why might Imran remember shouting while Parveen remembers speaking quietly?
qa.a: His fear and hurt likely made her words feel loud and harsh, while she remembers her own effort to stay calm with the neighbours over.

qa.q: Which step in the session helped, and why?
qa.a: Having each begin with "I remember it this way" while the other listened; it let both memories be heard without either being called a liar.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel when Imran nods at "You can always come home"?
qa.a: She would likely feel relief and tenderness, knowing her son heard the message she most wanted him to have.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenager and his mother each certain of different words in the same argument, their memories shaped by feeling.

passage:
School counsellor's note, family meeting, 7 March.
Amandeep, fifteen, and her mother, Charu, came in after a big fight last week about a missed tuition class. Each told me what was said. Amandeep: "She said I'm useless and I'll never amount to anything." Charu: "I said you were being careless, and that I was worried." Both were completely certain, and both were close to tears. I didn't try to decide who was right; nobody had recorded it. I explained that our memory of a heated moment gets reshaped by what we feel and by what we think about it afterwards. Then I asked each of them what they had felt in that moment. Amandeep: "Small." Charu: "Scared for her." They looked at each other for a long time. We'll meet again next Thursday.

qa.q: What was the fight about?
qa.a: A missed tuition class.

qa.q: Why is Amandeep so sure her mother called her useless?
qa.a: Amandeep felt small and hurt in the moment, and that feeling shaped the memory, so 'careless' may have been remembered as 'useless'.

qa.q: Why did the counsellor ask about feelings instead of deciding who was right?
qa.a: With no record, the exact words can't be settled, but sharing what they felt, small and scared, helps them understand each other.

qa.q: How does Charu remember the argument?
qa.a: Charu remembers saying Amandeep was being careless and that she was worried, and feels scared for her daughter.

grounding: Shows a teenager and a parent each certain of different words in an argument, with memories shaped by feelings.

Sunday night
Big fight with Pa. Two weeks ago, when I asked about the school trip to Sikkim, he said, "Yes, you can go." I KNOW he did. I remember exactly: he was reading the paper and he said yes. Today he says he said, "We'll see, if your marks are okay." I said he's changing the story. He said I'm hearing what I want to hear.
I asked Siddharth, who was there. He said he honestly doesn't remember the exact words, only that Pa was busy with the paper.
Now I'm lying here wondering. I was so excited that day. Maybe I heard 'we'll see' and my brain turned it into yes. Maybe Pa said yes and forgot. I don't know any more. Tomorrow I'll ask Pa if we can start again from now, instead of arguing about then.
Tenzin

On the bus home in Gothenburg, Ingrid replayed the argument from breakfast. Her father Pablo had said, "You're always on that phone and never help." She was sure. The words stung all day.

That evening, she brought it up. "You said I never help."

Pablo frowned. "I said, 'Could you help more with dishes?' That's it."

"No. You said never."

"Ingrid, I remember. I was tired, but I didn't say never."

They stared at each other. Ingrid felt her throat tighten. She had been angry all day about words he says he didn't say. Pablo rubbed his forehead. "Maybe I sounded harsher than I meant. And maybe you heard it bigger than I said it."

qa.q: What did Pablo say he asked Ingrid at breakfast?
qa.a: He said, "Could you help more with dishes?"

qa.q: How did Ingrid feel when her father disagreed about the words?
qa.a: She felt hurt and confused, her throat tightening, because she was sure and had been angry all day.

qa.q: Why did Pablo's last line calm things down?
qa.a: It admitted he might have sounded harsh and suggested both memories could be shaped by feelings, which calmed the argument.

qa.q: How might Pablo have felt hearing that Ingrid was upset all day?
qa.a: Pablo probably felt sad and a bit guilty that his tired words had hurt her so much.

grounding: A teenager and her father each remember a breakfast argument differently and both feel sure, as feelings shape memory.

In the school counsellor's room, Eshaan sat on one chair and his father Yogesh on the other. They had been sent there after shouting at each other in the car park.

"He said I'm a disappointment," Eshaan said, arms folded.

"I said I was disappointed in the marks," Yogesh said. "Not in you."

"You said me."

"I didn't!"

The counsellor waited. "Both of you were very upset. Upset people often remember the words that hurt most, and sometimes remember them stronger than they were said."

Eshaan looked at the floor. Yogesh sighed. "Whatever I said, I don't think you're a disappointment. I was scared about the exams."

Eshaan's shoulders dropped a little.

qa.q: Where had Eshaan and Yogesh shouted at each other?
qa.a: In the car park.

qa.q: Why was Eshaan so sure his father called him a disappointment?
qa.a: He felt hurt and ashamed, and those feelings shaped his memory of the words.

qa.q: What worked in the counsellor's approach?
qa.a: The counsellor didn't decide who was right but explained how upset people remember hurtful words, which let both of them soften.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel hearing his son thought he was called a disappointment?
qa.a: Yogesh probably felt upset and sad, which is why he clarified that he was scared, not disappointed in Eshaan.

grounding: A teenager and parent each remember a hurtful argument differently, both certain, as feelings reshape the memory.

"Manoj, you and your Papa both swear you're right about last night's fight. Let your Chaitanya Ajoba tell you something.
When your Papa was sixteen, during Ganpati, we argued about the late-night procession. For twenty years he has said I shouted, 'You're not going, full stop,' and slammed the door. And for twenty years I have remembered saying calmly, 'Let's talk about it tomorrow.'
Last Diwali your Ajji laughed at both of us. She said I did raise my voice, but I also said 'tomorrow'. And he did go the next year, with my permission. Neither of us remembered that part.
Each of us kept the piece that fitted our hurt. I remembered myself as reasonable. He remembered himself as wronged. Both of us were certain.
So before you fight about who said what, remember: certain is not the same as correct."

qa.q: Why did Papa remember the argument as "You're not going, full stop"?
qa.a: He felt hurt and wronged that night, and that feeling shaped the memory, so he kept the shouting and lost the word "tomorrow".

qa.q: At what point in the story could the two of them have cleared up the memory sooner?
qa.a: Any time in those twenty years they could have asked Ajji, or each said "this is how I remember it" instead of insisting, as her laugh finally made them do last Diwali.
